To test validation as well, build a ContinuumWorkflowModel.Node and call node.run(...) instead. Next: test and run your node.
Step 5 of 6About 10 minutes You ran the template unchanged in Step 1. Now run it again with your changes.
documents.s: Step 5: Test and run your node

documents.t: ./gradlew build This compiles every module, runs your unit tests, runs validateContinuumNodeAnnotations and builds the worker jar. To run one test class: ./gradlew :features:<repo>:test --tests "*WordCounterNodeModelTest" The annotation check validateContinuumNodeAnnotations fails the build when a class extends ProcessNodeModel or TriggerNodeModel without @ContinuumNode. If you see it fail, that's the cause.
Make sure the local stack from Step 1 is still up (docker compose ps in docker/), then: ./gradlew :worker:bootRun

The worker logs every node it found when it starts. Look for these two lines in the bootRun output: Registered process nodes: [com.acme.demo.node.WordCounterNodeModel] Registered trigger nodes: [] Your node's full class name should be in the list. You can also ask the worker over HTTP: curl http://localhost:8090/api/v1/node-repo Your Word Counter should be in the response. If it isn't, the build passed but the worker didn't find your node. Work through the checklist in Troubleshooting. Most often, one of these is wrong: the module isn't listed in worker/build.gradle.kts, the .imports file names the wrong class or @ComponentScan doesn't cover your package. (A missing @ContinuumNode is rarely the cause, because the build catches it.)

Open http://localhost:3002. Word Counter appears under Demo. Add a table source that has a text column, such as Create Table, and connect it to Word Counter. Open the Word Counter settings to see the form you defined, then run the workflow. Click the output port. Every row has a new word_count column. Open the node's help page in the Workbench. It should show your .doc.md content. If it reads "Documentation not found", see Step 4. Locally you don't need to set any environment variables: the worker's defaults match the local stack. When you deploy elsewhere, see the worker configuration reference. You've now changed the template into your own working worker. Next: ship it.
Step 6 of 6Needs repository secrets Shipping is mostly already set up in the template. This page explains what each piece does, what you need to provide and how to install the result.
Publish a GitHub Release After merging to main, create a release in the GitHub UI. That is what starts the publishing workflows.

Every change under features/ or worker/ needs: A new featureVersion in gradle.properties The chart's appVersion in charts/<repo>/Chart.yaml set to the same value CI enforces both on every pull request (validate-versions.yml). If your PR fails with "does not match featureVersion" or "featureVersion must be bumped", this is why. Example: # gradle.properties featureVersion=0.0.2 # charts/<repo>/Chart.yaml appVersion: "0.0.2" # Must match gradle.properties The Docker image tag defaults to the chart's appVersion, so the chart installs exactly the image built from the same release.

Workflow When What it does ci.yml PR, push to main ./gradlew build validate-versions.yml PR Checks the version rules above lint-test.yml PR touching charts/ ct lint on the Helm chart build-module.yml Manual Build one module, optionally publish it on-release.yml GitHub release published Libraries → Maven Central, worker → Docker Hub release.yml GitHub release published Attach the packaged Helm chart to the release and update the gh-pages index Workflows are triggered by a published release on-release.yml and release.yml run when you publish a GitHub Release (Repository → Releases → Create a new release). Pushing a tag or merging to main doesn't trigger them.

The release workflows read these from your repository's Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions: Secret Used for Required? MAVEN_CENTRAL_USERNAME, MAVEN_CENTRAL_PASSWORD Publishing libraries to Maven Central If publishing to Maven Central GPG_KEY_ID, GPG_PASSPHRASE, GPG_SECRET_KEY, GPG_PUBLIC_KEY Signing the published artifacts If publishing to Maven Central DOCKER_HUB_USERNAME, DOCKER_HUB_PASSWORD Pushing the worker image Yes, unless you change the image registry (see below)

Maven Central only accepts artifacts whose group is a namespace you have verified in the Central Portal. Your feature module's group is your <package> (for example com.acme.demo), so verify com.acme.demo's parent domain (com.acme) or use io.github.<your-user>. The Central Portal's namespace documentation explains the DNS or GitHub proof. Not publishing libraries? If your nodes only run in your own worker, you don't need Maven Central or the GPG secrets, and you don't need a verified namespace. Do both of these: In each feature module's continuum { } block, add publishToMavenCentral.set(false). In .github/workflows/on-release.yml, set publish_to_maven: false for those modules. Otherwise the release workflow tries to publish and fails on the missing secrets or namespace.

The worker image is built with Jib, so you don't need a Dockerfile and the CI runner doesn't need Docker. The target is jibToImage in worker/build.gradle.kts: continuum { continuumVersion.set(continuumPlatformVersion) jibToImage.set("acme/continuum-feature-demo:${project.version}") } on-release.yml runs ./gradlew :worker:jib, which pushes that image using the DOCKER_REPO_USERNAME and DOCKER_REPO_PASSWORD environment variables. The workflow fills them from DOCKER_HUB_USERNAME and DOCKER_HUB_PASSWORD. To use another registry (GitHub Container Registry, a private registry), put its full address in jibToImage (for example ghcr.io/acme/continuum-feature-demo:${project.version}), keep the same environment variable names, and change the env: lines of the "Push container image" step in on-release.yml to read your registry's credentials. Also change image.repository in the chart's values.yaml to match. If the registry is private, your cluster needs a pull secret. The template chart's global.imagePullSecrets value exists, but the Deployment template doesn't use it yet. Add this under spec.template.spec in charts/<repo>/templates/deployment.yaml: {{- with .Values.global.imagePullSecrets }} imagePullSecrets: {{- toYaml . | nindent 8 }} {{- end }} Then create the secret in the namespace (kubectl create secret docker-registry …) and list it in values.yaml: global: imagePullSecrets: - name: my-registry-secret

The chart wires your worker to the rest of the platform through the continuum: block in values.yaml. Three parts of it need your attention: Values What it is When to change it continuum.infra.* Addresses of the shared services: Temporal (host, port, namespace), Kafka (brokerList), the schema registry (url) and MinIO (endpoint). If you didn't install the continuum-infra chart under its default release name continuum-infra. Each address contains that release name. continuum.secrets.existingMinioSecret The name of the Kubernetes Secret that holds MinIO's root-user and root-password. Your chart doesn't create it; the continuum-platform chart does, named <release-name>-minio-secret. If you installed continuum-platform under a name other than continuum-platform. continuum.apiServer host and port of the platform's API server, where your worker registers its nodes. The default is the service continuum-platform-api-server on port 8080. Same: if the release name differs. Find the real service and secret names in your cluster with: kubectl get svc,secret -n continuum Your worker's own settings are under continuum.<valuesKey> (image, replicas, taskQueue, resources, autoscaling).

Before installing the chart, check the points that must agree: taskQueue in charts/<repo>/values.yaml matches node-task-queue in application.yaml taskQueue is globally unique (search other workers) image.repository in values.yaml matches what your release pushes The continuum.infra.*, secrets.existingMinioSecret and apiServer values match the release names in your cluster (see above) helm lint charts/<repo> passes

You can install from your working copy, or from the chart your release published. From the repository (good for a first test): helm install <repo> ./charts/<repo> -n continuum From your release: the release.yml workflow attaches the packaged chart (<repo>-<version>.tgz) to the GitHub release and adds it to the Helm index on your gh-pages branch. Enable GitHub Pages for the gh-pages branch in your repository settings (Settings → Pages), then: helm repo add <repo> https://<org>.github.io/<repo> helm repo update helm install <repo> <repo>/<repo> -n continuum For a private repository the index isn't publicly readable. Download the .tgz from the release and run helm install <repo> ./<repo>-0.0.2.tgz -n continuum instead. To roll out a new version, publish a new release and run helm upgrade. See Deployment for the full Kubernetes setup, and confirm the result by looking for your nodes in the Workbench, or check the worker's log for Registered process nodes: [...].

You don't need to set Kafka, MinIO or the API server addresses locally; the worker starter ships defaults that match the local stack. In Kubernetes, the chart sets these for you from values.yaml. Override them with environment variables when you deploy some other way: Variable Default Purpose CONTINUUM_NODE_TASK_QUEUE from application.yaml This worker's Temporal task queue TEMPORAL_SERVER_ADDRESS localhost:7233 Temporal frontend TEMPORAL_NAMESPACE default Temporal namespace CONTINUUM_API_SERVER_BASE_URL http://localhost:8080 Where nodes register CONTINUUM_KAFKA_MAIN_BROKER_LIST localhost:39092,localhost:39093,localhost:39094 Kafka brokers CONTINUUM_KAFKA_MAIN_SCHEMA_REGISTRY http://localhost:38080 Schema registry CONTINUUM_MINIO_ENDPOINT http://localhost:39000 Object storage for node data CONTINUUM_MINIO_USERNAME / _PASSWORD minioadmin MinIO credentials CONTINUUM_CREDENTIALS_SERVER_BASE_URL http://localhost:8083 Only for nodes that call getCredential(). The template chart doesn't set it; see Use a credential. CONTINUUM_CACHE_STORAGE_PATH ./.continuum-cache/workflow-data Local scratch folder SERVER_PORT 8090 Worker HTTP port (8080 belongs to the API server) You're done. Your worker is live and its nodes are available in the Workbench.

The build passes but your node isn't in the palette. Work down this list in order. Did the worker find the node? Look at the bootRun output for the line Registered process nodes: [...] (or Registered trigger nodes: [...] for a source node). If your class is listed, the worker is fine and the problem is on the Workbench or platform side: refresh the page and check that the local stack is healthy (docker compose ps in docker/). If the list is empty or your class is missing, continue with the checks below. Is the worker registered with the API server? Open http://localhost:8090/actuator/health, then run curl http://localhost:8090/api/v1/node-repo. The worker must be able to reach the API server (CONTINUUM_API_SERVER_BASE_URL, default http://localhost:8080). Is the module on the worker? worker/build.gradle.kts needs implementation(project(":features:<repo>")): grep "implementation(project" worker/build.gradle.kts Does the .imports file name your AutoConfigure class? The file is in your feature module, not the worker: cat features/<repo>/src/main/resources/META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports It must contain exactly <your.package>.AutoConfigure. Does @ComponentScan cover your node? In features/<repo>/src/main/kotlin/<your/package/path>/AutoConfigure.kt (or src/main/java/…/AutoConfigure.java), basePackages must include your node's package. The node class must be in that package or below. Is the class annotated? It needs @ContinuumNode, not @Component. ./gradlew build fails without it (validateContinuumNodeAnnotations), so if the build passed, this is rarely the cause. After fixing any of these, rebuild and restart the worker. Reloading the browser isn't enough. If it is still missing, check that the build output has no compilation errors and that the local stack is healthy. As a last resort, stop the worker, run docker compose restart in docker/, and start the worker again. Avoid docker compose down -v: it deletes the stack's data volumes.
documents.s: My node doesn't show up in the Workbench

documents.t: Look at the worker console (the bootRun output). Your execute() exception and stack trace are there. A node that fails and then runs again is being retried. If the cause can't change between attempts (bad settings, an unconnected port), throw NodeRuntimeException(isRetriable = false, …); see Errors, retries and progress. Reproduce it in a unit test with the same settings and input rows. This is faster than rerunning a workflow.
documents.s: My node appears but fails when it runs

documents.t: Symptom Cause and fix Plugin [id: 'org.projectcontinuum.worker', version: '…'] was not found continuumPlatformVersion in gradle.properties isn't a released version on Maven Central, or mavenCentral() is missing from pluginManagement.repositories in settings.gradle.kts. Unresolved reference 'databind' / 'ObjectMapper' Jackson 2 imports. Use tools.jackson.core.type.TypeReference and tools.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper, not com.fasterxml.jackson.*. validateContinuumNodeAnnotations FAILED A class extends ProcessNodeModel or TriggerNodeModel without @ContinuumNode. Unsupported class file major version or invalid source release: 21 The build runs on the wrong JDK. Run java -version and ./gradlew --version; both must report 21. Set JAVA_HOME to a JDK 21 and stop old daemons with ./gradlew --stop. Java heap space, GC overhead limit exceeded or the Gradle daemon dies during compilation Gradle needs more memory. The template sets org.gradle.jvmargs=-Xmx4g -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=1g in gradle.properties. Keep that line; if you removed it, put it back, and make sure the machine has the memory to spare. Port 8080 was already in use on bootRun The local API server uses 8080. Keep server.port: ${SERVER_PORT:8090} in application.yaml. Worker starts but logs connection errors for Kafka, Temporal or MinIO The local stack isn't running or isn't healthy. Run docker compose ps in docker/ and wait until every container is healthy. The stack needs about 8 GB of RAM, so raise Docker Desktop's memory limit if containers keep restarting or get killed. Worker starts but registers [] for both process and trigger nodes The worker didn't load your module. See the checklist above, steps 3 to 5. NoSuchBeanDefinitionException or UnsatisfiedDependencyException for your node at start-up The node's constructor asks for a bean Spring can't provide. Nodes can take ObjectMapper; anything else must be a bean from the worker. If in doubt, make the constructor empty. A node fails at random, or runs on the wrong worker Several workers share a task queue. Temporal gives work to whichever worker polls first, including one that doesn't have the node, and nothing warns you. Set a unique node-task-queue in application.yaml and taskQueue in the chart. IllegalArgumentException: Unsupported type while writing A cell value isn't a supported type (String, Int, Long, Float, Double, Boolean, List, Map or SVG). Convert it, or leave the key out instead of using null. See Reading and writing rows. CredentialsNotFoundException The credential name in the node's settings doesn't exist on the credentials server. In the local stack there is no credentials server at all; see Use a credential. Help page reads "Documentation not found" The .doc.md path doesn't match the node's full package and class name. For com.acme.demo.node.MyNodeModel it is src/main/resources/com/acme/demo/node/MyNodeModel.doc.md. See Step 4.

Symptom Cause and fix Helm: template: no template associated with name A rename in charts/ was only partly done. Every include "…" must match a define in _helpers.tpl. See Step 3. PR fails validate-versions Bump featureVersion in gradle.properties and set the chart's appVersion to the same value. See Step 6. Release workflow doesn't start on-release.yml and release.yml run on a published GitHub Release, not on a tag or a merge. See Step 6. Maven Central deploy fails with a namespace or signing error The group (your package) isn't a namespace you verified in the Central Portal, or the GPG secrets are missing. Verify the namespace, or switch publishing off; see Step 6. Jib push fails with 401 Unauthorized or denied DOCKER_HUB_USERNAME / DOCKER_HUB_PASSWORD are missing or wrong, or the account can't push to the repository named in jibToImage. See Step 6. Pod stuck in ImagePullBackOff The image name or tag in the chart doesn't exist, or the registry is private and the pod has no pull secret. See Step 6. Pod stuck in Init An init container is waiting for Kafka, Temporal or the API server. Its address in continuum.infra.* or continuum.apiServer doesn't match a real service. Check with kubectl get svc -n continuum and see Step 6. Pod fails to start because a Secret is missing continuum.secrets.existingMinioSecret names a Secret that doesn't exist in the namespace. See Step 6. Saved workflows break after a rename You renamed or moved a node class. The full class name is the node's identity in saved workflows, so don't rename classes after shipping.

Feature workers (continuum-feature-*) are not part of continuum-platform-core — each lives in its own repo with its own build and release pipeline, and can be deployed as an independent worker service into the same namespace as the core platform. This is intentional: new capabilities ship as new workers, not as changes to existing ones. See Node Model & Feature Registration for how a worker's nodes get discovered by the platform at runtime.

The Continuum Gradle plugin turns an empty Gradle module into a Continuum feature library or a runnable worker. You apply one plugin ID, set a version, and get Spring Boot, the Continuum libraries, tests, publishing and container images configured for you. 4 plugin IDsKotlin or JavaPlatform 0.0.20 Use this page when you start a project from scratch. If you would rather start from a working repository, clone the template instead (Create New Nodes); the template uses exactly the setup described here.

The plugin ships as one artifact, org.projectcontinuum.core:continuum-gradle-plugin, which registers four plugin IDs: Plugin ID Use it for Language org.projectcontinuum.feature A library module that contains nodes Kotlin org.projectcontinuum.feature-java A library module that contains nodes Java org.projectcontinuum.worker The runnable worker (Spring Boot app) that loads your feature modules Kotlin org.projectcontinuum.worker-java The runnable worker Java A worker plugin first applies the matching feature plugin and then adds the application parts, so everything a feature module gets, a worker gets too. You can mix languages. The template has a Kotlin worker that loads both a Kotlin and a Java feature module. Every plugin gives you: Dependencies: Spring Boot starters, continuum-commons, Jackson 3 and the test libraries, with Spring Boot, Spring Cloud and Temporal BOMs imported. Build setup: a Java 21 toolchain, JUnit 5, sources and Javadoc jars, and Maven Central, Confluent and local Maven repositories. A build-time check that every node class carries @ContinuumNode (details). Publishing to Maven Central through JReleaser (details). The worker plugins add the continuum-worker-springboot-starter, the Spring Boot application plugin (bootJar, bootRun) and, when you ask for it, a container image built with Jib (details).

This walks through a minimal repository with one feature module and one worker. It uses Kotlin; for Java, swap the plugin IDs as noted. You need: JDK 21. Use Gradle 8.14, the version the template's wrapper pins and the one this page was checked with.

my-continuum-worker/ ├── gradle.properties ├── settings.gradle.kts ├── build.gradle.kts ├── gradlew, gradlew.bat, gradle/ ← the Gradle wrapper ├── features/ │ └── my-feature/ │ ├── build.gradle.kts │ └── src/main/… ← your nodes └── worker/ ├── build.gradle.kts └── src/main/… ← the Spring Boot app For the wrapper, copy gradlew, gradlew.bat and the gradle/ folder from the template, or run gradle wrapper --gradle-version 8.14 if you have Gradle installed.

Put the Continuum version in gradle.properties so the plugin version and the library version can't drift apart: # gradle.properties continuumPlatformVersion=0.0.20 featureVersion=0.0.1 # Gradle needs more memory to compile with Spring Boot 4 and Kotlin 2.2 org.gradle.jvmargs=-Xmx4g -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=1g continuumPlatformVersion is the version of the plugin and of the Continuum libraries it adds. They are released together, so use the same value for both.

// settings.gradle.kts pluginManagement { val continuumPlatformVersion: String by settings repositories { mavenCentral() gradlePluginPortal() } plugins { id("org.projectcontinuum.feature") version continuumPlatformVersion id("org.projectcontinuum.worker") version continuumPlatformVersion // Java modules: also declare feature-java and/or worker-java } } rootProject.name = "my-continuum-worker" include(":features:my-feature") include(":worker") Declaring the versions once here means the module build files apply the plugins by ID only. Add mavenLocal() to the repositories only when you are testing a plugin build you made yourself. The root build.gradle.kts can stay empty. The template adds plugins { id("org.jreleaser") version "1.23.0" apply false } there; a multi-module build without it also configured and built in our checks, so it is optional.

// features/my-feature/build.gradle.kts plugins { id("org.projectcontinuum.feature") } group = "com.acme.demo" description = "My Continuum nodes" version = property("featureVersion").toString() continuum { continuumVersion.set(property("continuumPlatformVersion").toString()) } Always set continuumVersion continuumVersion has a built-in default of 0.0.6, which is not the current platform. If you leave it out, the module quietly builds against old Continuum libraries and you get confusing compile errors. Set it in every module that applies a Continuum plugin. group and version matter: they become the Maven coordinates when you publish the module. For a Java module use id("org.projectcontinuum.feature-java").

The worker finds your nodes through Spring auto-configuration. Add one class and one file to the feature module: // features/my-feature/src/main/kotlin/com/acme/demo/AutoConfigure.kt package com.acme.demo import org.springframework.context.annotation.ComponentScan import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration @Configuration @ComponentScan(basePackages = ["com.acme.demo"]) class AutoConfigure # features/my-feature/src/main/resources/META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports com.acme.demo.AutoConfigure Now write your nodes in com.acme.demo or a sub-package. Step 4: Write your node covers the node class, help page and tests.

// worker/build.gradle.kts plugins { id("org.projectcontinuum.worker") } group = "com.acme.demo.worker" description = "My Continuum worker" version = property("featureVersion").toString() continuum { continuumVersion.set(property("continuumPlatformVersion").toString()) } dependencies { implementation(project(":features:my-feature")) } Add the application class and its configuration: // worker/src/main/kotlin/com/acme/demo/worker/App.kt package com.acme.demo.worker import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication import org.springframework.boot.runApplication @SpringBootApplication class App fun main(args: Array<String>) { runApplication<App>(*args) } # worker/src/main/resources/application.yaml spring.application.name: my-continuum-worker # 8080 is taken by the API server in the local stack server.port: ${SERVER_PORT:8090} spring: temporal: namespace: ${TEMPORAL_NAMESPACE:default} connection: target: ${TEMPORAL_SERVER_ADDRESS:localhost:7233} workersAutoDiscovery: packages: - org.projectcontinuum.core.worker.starter continuum.core: worker: # Must be unique per worker node-task-queue: ${CONTINUUM_NODE_TASK_QUEUE:MY_CONTINUUM_WORKER_TASK_QUEUE} The worker starter supplies defaults for Kafka, MinIO and the API server that match the local stack, so these are the only settings you must provide. The Step 6 reference lists the environment variables you can override, and the unique task queue rule is explained in Step 3.

./gradlew build ./gradlew :worker:bootRun bootRun needs the local Continuum stack; see Step 5 for starting it and seeing your nodes in the Workbench. A successful start logs Registered process nodes: [...] with your node classes.

Every module that applies a Continuum plugin gets a continuum { } block. All properties are optional, except that you should always set continuumVersion. continuum { continuumVersion.set("0.0.20") publishToMavenCentral.set(false) jibToImage.set("acme/my-worker:${project.version}") } Property Type Default Applies to What it does continuumVersion String 0.0.6 all Version of continuum-commons and, for workers, continuum-worker-springboot-starter. Set this. continuumGroup String org.projectcontinuum.core all Maven group of those two Continuum artifacts. Change only if you use a fork. useKotlin Boolean true for feature/worker, false for the -java plugins all Chosen for you by the plugin ID. It decides which dependencies are added (Kotlin or Java Jackson and test libraries) and where the node check looks for classes. Leave it alone. springBootVersion String 4.0.6 all Version of the spring-boot-dependencies BOM. The Spring Boot Gradle plugin version is fixed by the Continuum plugin. springCloudVersion String 2025.1.1 all Version of the Spring Cloud BOM. temporalVersion String 1.28.0 all Version of the Temporal BOM. jacksonVersion String 3.1.2 all Version of the Jackson 3 artifacts (tools.jackson.*) added directly. awsSdkVersion String 2.30.7 workers Version of the AWS SDK BOM. publishToMavenCentral Boolean true all Configures signing and the Maven Central deployment (details). Set false if you don't publish the module. jibFromImage String eclipse-temurin:21-jre workers Base image for the container. jibToImage String none workers Target image, for example acme/my-worker:1.0.0. If unset, no container image is configured at all. The defaults are the ones in plugin 0.0.20; later releases may move them. Normally you only touch continuumVersion, publishToMavenCentral and jibToImage and leave the rest, because the platform is tested against its own defaults. Values are read after your build script runs The plugins add dependencies and BOMs after your build script is evaluated, so set versions through continuum { } rather than trying to edit the generated dependency lines.

feature (Kotlin) feature-java Language plugins org.jetbrains.kotlin.jvm and org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.spring (Kotlin 2.2.0) java-library Always applied Spring dependency management, maven-publish, JReleaser the same Compiler options -Xjsr305=strict none JSON library tools.jackson.module:jackson-module-kotlin, kotlin-reflect tools.jackson.core:jackson-databind Test libraries kotlin-test-junit5, mockito-kotlin junit-jupiter, mockito-core You don't declare Kotlin or Spring Boot plugin versions yourself; the Continuum plugin brings them. Both feature plugins also set up: Toolchain: Java 21, plus withSourcesJar() and withJavadocJar(), which Maven Central requires. Repositories: mavenLocal(), mavenCentral() and the Confluent repository (packages.confluent.io/maven). Tests: every Test task uses the JUnit Platform. Dependencies (implementation): spring-boot-starter, spring-boot-autoconfigure, spring-boot-starter-web, spring-boot-starter-actuator and continuum-commons. Test dependencies: spring-boot-starter-test and the JUnit launcher, plus the language-specific libraries above. BOMs: spring-boot-dependencies, temporal-bom and spring-cloud-dependencies. The node check (validateContinuumNodeAnnotations) and publishing, described below.

A worker plugin applies its feature plugin and then adds: the org.springframework.boot plugin, which gives you bootJar and bootRun; the software.amazon.awssdk:bom BOM; continuum-worker-springboot-starter as an implementation dependency; Jib, only if jibToImage is set. Because a worker is also a feature module, it is publishable too. In practice you publish its container image, not its jar; the template's release workflow publishes libraries and the worker image separately (Step 6).

Every node class needs @ContinuumNode, and a missing annotation is easy to overlook until the node doesn't show up. The plugins catch this at build time with the task validateContinuumNodeAnnotations. It is in the verification group and runs before classes, so ./gradlew build, test and bootRun all trigger it. It scans the compiled classes of the module (build/classes/kotlin/main or build/classes/java/main) for concrete classes that implement ContinuumNodeModel (which ProcessNodeModel and TriggerNodeModel do) and lack the annotation. It skips abstract classes, interfaces, inner classes and anonymous classes. If continuum-commons isn't on the classpath, it does nothing. A missing annotation fails the build with a message that names the class: Execution failed for task ':features:my-feature:validateContinuumNodeAnnotations'. > Continuum Node Annotation Validation Failed The following classes implement ContinuumNodeModel but are missing the @ContinuumNode annotation: - com.acme.demo.BadNodeModel Add @ContinuumNode to the class and rebuild.

A feature module can be published to Maven Central so other workers can depend on your nodes. The plugin configures this in two stages. Stage locally. A mavenJava publication (the jar, sources jar and Javadoc jar, with a full POM) is published to a repository called localStaging at build/staging-deploy: ./gradlew :features:my-feature:publish Deploy. JReleaser signs the staged files with PGP and uploads them to the Maven Central Portal: ./gradlew :features:my-feature:jreleaserDeploy The Maven coordinates come from the module's group, name and version. The POM links to your repository using the GITHUB_REPOSITORY environment variable (set automatically on GitHub Actions) or, locally, a repoName property in gradle.properties (for example repoName=my-org/my-repo). The POM also lists a fixed developer and the Apache 2.0 license. The developer entry is Continuum Developer, and the extension has no setting to change it.

Variable Used by Purpose JRELEASER_MAVENCENTRAL_SONATYPE_USERNAME, JRELEASER_MAVENCENTRAL_SONATYPE_TOKEN jreleaserDeploy Maven Central Portal account JRELEASER_GPG_PASSPHRASE, JRELEASER_GPG_SECRET_KEY, JRELEASER_GPG_PUBLIC_KEY jreleaserDeploy Signing key MAVEN_REPO_USERNAME, MAVEN_REPO_PASSWORD publish, for -SNAPSHOT versions only Sonatype snapshots repository The template's on-release.yml maps its repository secrets to these variables; see Step 6. Signing is always on, so jreleaserDeploy fails without the GPG variables. Your module's group must be a namespace you have verified in the Maven Central Portal.
If the module's version ends in -SNAPSHOT, publish also pushes to the Sonatype snapshots repository (central.sonatype.com/repository/maven-snapshots/) using the MAVEN_REPO_* variables.

If a module is only used inside your own worker, don't publish it: continuum { publishToMavenCentral.set(false) } This leaves out the signing and Maven Central deployment settings. The maven-publish and JReleaser plugins stay applied, so the tasks still exist, but don't run jreleaserDeploy for that module. Remember to turn it off in your release workflow as well.

Worker plugins build container images with Jib, so you need no Dockerfile and no Docker daemon in CI. Jib is opt-in. Set jibToImage and the plugin applies Jib and configures it; leave it unset and no Jib tasks exist. continuum { continuumVersion.set(property("continuumPlatformVersion").toString()) jibToImage.set("acme/my-worker:${project.version}") // jibFromImage.set("eclipse-temurin:21-jre") // the default } Setting Value Base image jibFromImage (default eclipse-temurin:21-jre) Target image jibToImage Registry login DOCKER_REPO_USERNAME and DOCKER_REPO_PASSWORD environment variables; empty if unset Build and push with: ./gradlew :worker:jib # push to the registry ./gradlew :worker:jibDockerBuild # build into your local Docker daemon ./gradlew :worker:jibBuildTar # build a tarball To use a registry other than Docker Hub, put its full address in jibToImage (for example ghcr.io/acme/my-worker:1.0.0) and set the two environment variables to that registry's credentials.

Task Added by What it does validateContinuumNodeAnnotations all Fails the build if a node class lacks @ContinuumNode. Runs before classes. publish all Stages the library into build/staging-deploy (and Sonatype snapshots for -SNAPSHOT versions). publishToMavenLocal all Installs the library into ~/.m2. Useful for trying a module in another project. jreleaserDeploy all Signs and deploys the staged artifacts to Maven Central. Needs publishToMavenCentral left true. bootRun workers Starts the worker from Gradle. bootJar workers Builds the executable Spring Boot jar. jib, jibDockerBuild, jibBuildTar workers, only when jibToImage is set Build the container image. Run ./gradlew :worker:tasks --all to see everything, including the other JReleaser tasks.

Symptom Cause and fix Plugin [id: 'org.projectcontinuum.feature', version: '…'] was not found The version isn't a released one, or pluginManagement.repositories in settings.gradle.kts lacks mavenCentral(). Compile errors for Continuum classes you know exist, or the wrong API continuumVersion isn't set and defaulted to 0.0.6. Set it in every module's continuum { } block. validateContinuumNodeAnnotations FAILED A class extends ProcessNodeModel or TriggerNodeModel without @ContinuumNode. See above. Unresolved reference on ObjectMapper or TypeReference Jackson 2 imports. The plugin adds Jackson 3; import tools.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper and tools.jackson.core.type.TypeReference. Unsupported class file major version or a toolchain error Gradle isn't running on JDK 21. Check java -version and ./gradlew --version, set JAVA_HOME, and run ./gradlew --stop. Gradle daemon runs out of memory Add org.gradle.jvmargs=-Xmx4g -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=1g to gradle.properties. Task 'jib' not found jibToImage isn't set in that module's continuum { } block, so Jib was never applied. jreleaserDeploy fails on signing or credentials The GPG or Sonatype environment variables are missing. Provide them, or set publishToMavenCentral.set(false). jib fails with 401 Unauthorized DOCKER_REPO_USERNAME / DOCKER_REPO_PASSWORD are missing, or the account can't push to the image name in jibToImage. The worker starts but registers no nodes Not a plugin problem: check the AutoConfiguration.imports file and @ComponentScan. See Troubleshooting.

The source is in the continuum-gradle-plugin module of continuum-platform-core. Its version always equals the platform version. To pick up a new platform release, change continuumPlatformVersion in gradle.properties and rebuild.

Project Continuum is an open-source, browser-native visual workflow platform — inspired by KNIME, built for the cloud. You design workflows as a drag-and-drop graph of nodes, and the platform runs them durably: a crashed worker, a dead Kafka broker, or a dropped connection doesn't lose your progress. Apache 2.0Browser-native IDEPowered by TemporalParquet data passing No desktop install — the entire IDE runs in your browser.

🖥️Browser-native canvas A full IDE experience (Eclipse Theia + React Flow) with zero install. 🛡️Crash-proof execution Powered by Temporal, workflows survive process crashes, network failures, and restarts. Every step retries automatically. ⚡Real-time streaming Watch workflows execute step-by-step. Kafka streams events to your browser via MQTT over WebSockets. No polling, no refresh. 🧱Columnar data passing Nodes exchange Apache Parquet tables, not JSON blobs. Fast, compressed, query-ready. 🧩Extensible by design Add capabilities by deploying new worker services, not by modifying existing ones. Zero downtime, zero coupling. 🔓Open source Apache 2.0 licensed, from the workbench to the workers.

A workflow is a directed graph of nodes. When you hit Execute, the orchestration service interprets that graph as a durable Temporal workflow.
